newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SINGAPORE ECONOMY TO GROW 6-7 PCT IN 1997 - PM GOH.
newsitem.headline: SINGAPORE ECONOMY TO GROW 6-7 PCT IN 1997 - PM GOH.

text.p: Singapore's economy is expanding faster than expected and will grow at between six and seven percent in 1997, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said on Friday.
The government had previously forecast that Gross Domestic Product (GDP) would grow between five and seven percent. Economists predicted the final figure would be twoards the upper end of that range.

"MTI (the Ministry of Trade and Industry) expects the economy to continue to strengthen in the second half of 1997. For the full year MTI has revised its forecast to between six and seven percent growth," Goh said in a National Day broadcast.
Goh said the economy grew by 5.9 percent in the first half of 1997 compared to 8.9 percent int he same period of the previous year.
But he said it picked up in the second quarter expanding 7.8 percent compared to 7.0 percent in the second quarter of 1996.

"Manufacturing is recovering from the slowdown. All other sectors did well. Reflecting our strong fundamentals, we attracted Singapore $4.8 billion of manufacturing investments in the first half of this year," Goh said in the televised speech.
Singapore's economy grew at seven percent in 1996, 8.8 percent in 1995 and by double-digits in the preceding two years.
Goh said globalisation and technology were two of the main forces driving world economics and that Singapore was well placed to take advantage of this.
"We have always been an open economy, exporting to world markets. We have upgraded our technology, focused on IT and built up a headstart," he said.
"We are well placed to become a premier business node in our region. We must make the most of this lead, to consolidate our basic strengths and acquire new ones."
But Goh said competition from other countries in Asia, including Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea was intensifying.
"They are upgrading their infrastructure, training their workforce and offering tax incentives for foreign investments. Competition for investments, jobs and markets will intensify," he said.
